The Common myna (Acridotheres tristis) displays a robust reproductive capacity characterized by a clutch size of 4.5 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 4.5 eggs per nesting attempt] and the production of three clutches each year [F_R_i = three clutches each year], a strategy that allows for substantial annual recruitment in its introduced ranges. The successful initiation of a first brood typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], when conditions align with the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the temperature at which active metabolic rates and foraging efficiency appear optimized. This timing ensures that young are provisioned during periods of peak insect abundance, a critical factor given the species predominantly insectivorous diet during the breeding season.

The embryonic development period, or incubation duration, proceeds over 17.5 days [ab = 17.5 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]; this value is an estimate derived from captive-breeding records of Sturnidae. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably low wet weight of only 4.2 grams [Wwb = 4.2 grams], reflecting the yolk-dependent nature of the embryonated egg and the limited reserves available to the newly hatched chick. This modest birth mass necessitates an intensive period of biparental provisioning, with both the incubating adult and its mate delivering food to the rapidly developing brood.

Under the sustained thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that typify the active foraging periods during the breeding season, the nestling chick undergoes a predictable sequence of developmental milestones. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and initial attempts at first foraging, occurs 23 days after hatching [tx = 23 days after hatching], a period during which the chick's mass increases many-fold at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The subsequent attainment of puberty, defined here as the onset of functional spermatogenesis in males and ovarian follicle development in females, occurs at 69 days after hatching [tp = 69 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime, though actual first breeding typically occurs much later at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species. The ultimate wet weight attained by females averages approximately 113 grams [Wwi = approximately 113 grams], though literature values from the Animal Diversity Web report a broader range of 82 to 143 grams for this sex, reflecting geographical variation in resource availability. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males is consistently higher, with a mean of approximately 125 grams [Wwi = approximately 125 grams]. This disparity in asymptotic mass likely reflects differential selective pressures on males for territorial defense and mate acquisition versus the energetic demands of egg production and incubation in females.

Maximum recorded longevity in this species is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], based on mark-recapture studies of stable populations in India, where the birds experience the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] during the active season. This lifespan is relatively moderate for a passerine of its size. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is approximately 7.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 7.1 grams], a value that represents a substantial maternal investment relative to the 4.2 gram [Wwb = 4.2 gram] mass of the hatchling, indicating that a significant portion of the egg's initial mass is composed of albumen and yolk reserves consumed during development. The combination of three clutches each year [F_R_i = three clutches each year], each containing 4.5 eggs [N_R_i = each containing 4.5 eggs], yields a high annual reproductive output that, together with broad dietary tolerance and aggressive territorial behavior, positions this species as one of the most successful avian colonizers of disturbed habitats globally.
